approach: EU AI Act Art. 51(2): 10^25 FLOP presumption
T1_reason: A single rebuttable in/out presumption at 10^25 FLOP.
T2_reason: Outsiders can estimate training compute from public disclosures. Epoch AI does so, flags confidence levels, and reports a mean absolute error of about 2.2x for benchmark-imputed estimates. Legal status still depends on the developer's own count or report.
T3_reason: The quantity (cumulative training FLOP), the estimation procedure (hardware or architecture method, with exclusions) and the error tolerance (±30%) are all specified, though in the Commission guidelines rather than in Article 51 itself.
T4_reason: A training-compute count does not register gains from post-training, inference-time compute or scaffolding. Treasury's 2026 NPRM makes the same point, and post-training gains are worth more than 5x compute.
T5_reason: Training compute correlates strongly with WMDP hazardous-knowledge scores (|r| about 0.83 to 0.91). That is correlational evidence with a harm-evaluation proxy only, and nothing links the 10^25 line itself to realized harm.
T6_reason: Enacted EU regulation in force; fines are enforceable from 2 August 2026.

approach: US state laws: 10^26 FLOP + revenue (CA SB 53, NY RAISE, IL, CT)
T1_reason: A model is in or out at 10^26. The revenue line sorts developers, not systems.
T2_reason: Outsiders can estimate training compute from public disclosures. Epoch AI does so, flags confidence levels, and reports a mean absolute error of about 2.2x for benchmark-imputed estimates. Legal status still depends on the developer's own count or report. Revenue is public for listed companies.
T3_reason: The statute specifies the quantity (integer or floating-point operations, including fine-tuning and material modifications) but no counting procedure and no error tolerance.
T4_reason: California SB 53 counts compute used for fine-tuning, reinforcement learning and other later modifications toward its 10^26 threshold (Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code 22757.11(i)(2)); post-training that uses little compute, and inference-time compute, are still not counted.
T5_reason: Only correlational evidence links training compute to a hazardous-knowledge benchmark proxy (WMDP). Nothing validates 10^26 against harm.
T6_reason: SB 53 has been in force since January 1, 2026. NY, Illinois and Connecticut laws are enacted, with phased dates in 2026 to 2028.

approach: South Korea AI Framework Act: compute safety duty
T1_reason: A conjunction of three in/out criteria.
T2_reason: Compute can be estimated externally. The other two criteria ('most advanced technology', 'widespread and significant impact') are qualitative judgments.
T3_reason: The quantity (at least 10^26 FLOP, cumulative) is specified, and the calculation method is delegated to a ministerial notice. No error tolerance is stated.
T4_reason: The compute criterion is training-only. The 'most advanced technology' criterion is undefined.
T5_reason: Compute has only the generic correlational link to hazardous-knowledge benchmarks. Nothing validates the three-part conjunction.
T6_reason: Enacted statute and presidential decree, in force since January 22, 2026.

approach: Scher et al. draft treaty: three compute bands
T1_reason: A few ordered bands: free below 10^22, monitored up to 10^24, prohibited above, plus a separate 10^23 post-training cap.
T2_reason: Outsiders can estimate compute, but the treaty's verification rests on declarations, chip tracking and on-site inspection.
T3_reason: The quantity and counting convention (FP16-equivalent or total operations, whichever is higher) and the reporting and inspection procedure are specified. No error tolerance is given.
T4_reason: A 10^23 post-training cap and a technique whitelist address post-training. Methods that do not change parameters, such as prompting, and inference-time compute are explicitly outside the 'methods' definition.
T5_reason: Only the generic correlation between compute and hazardous-knowledge benchmarks exists. The authors give a judgment rationale, not evidence.
T6_reason: An academic proposal (arXiv draft, v3 May 8, 2026), not adopted by any state.

T1_reason: A single in/out reporting trigger, with a 10^23 variant for biological-sequence models.
T2_reason: Compute can be estimated externally, but reporting depended on developers.
T3_reason: Only the quantity (integer or floating-point operations) was specified, with no counting method or error tolerance.
T4_reason: Training compute only.
T5_reason: Generic correlational evidence between compute and hazardous-knowledge benchmarks only. The threshold was set by calibration, not harm evidence.
T6_reason: Rescinded January 20, 2025 by EO 14148. It was a binding executive order from October 2023 to January 2025.

approach: US Treasury Part 850 compute tiers (current rule)
T1_reason: Three ordered tiers: not covered, notifiable above 10^23, prohibited above 10^25 (above 10^24 for biological-sequence models).
T2_reason: Compute can be estimated from public information, but often not for the PRC developers the rule targets. The US investor must conduct diligence on the target's compute.
T3_reason: Only the quantity ('computational operations (e.g., integer or floating-point operations)') is specified, with no counting method or error.
T4_reason: Treasury itself concluded that gains now come from post-training and inference-time compute that the compute tiers miss.
T5_reason: Only the generic correlation between compute and hazardous-knowledge benchmarks exists. Treasury cites no harm validation for 10^25.
T6_reason: Part 850 is a binding final rule, effective January 2, 2025. Proposed Part 851 would drop compute.

T1_reason: A continuous scale (task length in human minutes at 50% or 80% success).
T2_reason: METR measures deployed models through API access, so no developer cooperation is needed after release. But most of the suite is private to prevent contamination, so others cannot fully replicate it, and pre-release measurement needs developer-granted access.
T3_reason: Tasks are specified (228 in TH1.1, with human baselines), as is the procedure (logistic fit on log human time over repeated runs per task), with bootstrap confidence intervals over task families, tasks and runs. The reliability limit (16 h) is stated.
T4_reason: It measures the elicited system with its scaffold, so post-training and inference-time gains register. Results depend on scaffold and token budget: third-party cyber-horizon work shows large shifts from 2M to 10M+ tokens.
T5_reason: No published study shows that a model's horizon predicts realized harm or a validated harm proxy. METR's 8 h and 40 h concern thresholds are argued, not empirically validated. The horizon correlates 0.94 with Epoch's general capability index, and general capability correlates with WMDP, but that link is indirect.
T6_reason: No law or framework uses the horizon as a trigger. It is reported in developer system cards and METR evaluation reports.

T1_reason: Binary designation as a 'covered frontier model'.
T2_reason: The benchmark and threshold are classified, and the NSA Director alone makes the designation.
T3_reason: No tasks, procedure or error are public.
T4_reason: It is a capability benchmark on the model, so in principle it captures post-training gains. Whether scaffolding or inference compute is included is not public.
T5_reason: There is no public evidence, and a secret threshold cannot be validated publicly.
T6_reason: An executive order binding on agencies, but developer participation is voluntary. Section 3(c) disclaims any mandatory licensing or preclearance.

T1_reason: Pass/fail gates on individual metrics. The current version has undefined 'risk tiers'.
T2_reason: MASK is public and can be run on Grok via the API. The restricted bio/chem query benchmark is internal (built with SecureBio), and the current version names no benchmarks.
T3_reason: The August and December 2025 versions specify benchmarks and numeric rates but no sample size or error. The June 2026 version specifies none.
T4_reason: It is measured on the model as deployed, with safeguards, so post-training is captured. Elicitation, scaffolding and inference settings are unstated.
T5_reason: No evidence that MASK dishonesty or the restricted-query answer rate predicts realized harm or a validated proxy.
T6_reason: A company policy. SB 53 makes a large frontier developer's non-compliance with its own published framework subject to civil penalties, which gives the framework some legal force in California.

T1_reason: Two ordered levels (High, Critical) per Tracked Category.
T2_reason: The determination uses internal indicative thresholds and SAG judgment. Outsiders can run public evaluations but cannot place a model against OpenAI's thresholds.
T3_reason: Tracked categories and qualitative thresholds are specified, with Scalable Evaluations and Deep Dives. No indicative cutoffs, sample sizes or error are given in the framework.
T4_reason: It applies to covered systems, including internal agentic systems, and new Capabilities Reports are required on significant changes. Elicitation adequacy is self-judged, and sandbagging is only a Research Category.
T5_reason: No published evidence that crossing High or Critical predicts realized harm or a validated proxy. The September 2026 Astra Critical designation and the reported testing incident are anecdotal.
T6_reason: A company policy. SB 53 makes non-compliance with a large frontier developer's own published framework penalizable.

approach: US CAISI capability score and frontier lag
T1_reason: Continuous Elo-like scale (e.g. DeepSeek V4 Pro about 800 ±28) where 'every 200-point increase … equates to a 3x increase in the odds of solving a given task'.
T2_reason: CAISI served the open-weight DeepSeek V4 itself on cloud GPUs and reproduced self-reported results; closed U.S. reference models were evaluated through access CAISI already had.
T3_reason: 1PL IRT over nine named benchmarks with equal domain weights and 95% CIs, but two benchmarks (PortBench, ARC-AGI-2 semi-private) are non-public and the full method write-up was still pending, so outsiders cannot replicate it.
T4_reason: It scores deployed post-trained models with agent scaffolds, but fixes token budgets and scaffolding, so extra inference-time compute or bespoke harnesses are outside the score.
T5_reason: The reports frame results as capability, cost and censorship comparisons and draw no risk conclusion even from the cyber CTF scores.
T6_reason: An official government evaluation with no legal consequence attached; it is not a regulatory threshold.

T1_reason: A single continuous IRT scale anchored at Claude 3.5 Sonnet = 130 and GPT-5 = 150.
T2_reason: 'The only data we use is model performance on benchmarks'; no compute, training or developer data are needed.
T3_reason: Bayesian IRT with per-benchmark difficulty and slope, 90% credible intervals and explicit inclusion rules, but the benchmark set and values change by methodology version.
T4_reason: It scores released models as benchmarked, including reasoning modes, but elicitation settings vary across the benchmark sources it aggregates.
T5_reason: The methodology makes no statement linking ECI to risk or harm.
T6_reason: A research index not referenced by any binding or voluntary governance instrument.

T1_reason: Ordered cyber difficulty levels, 50% task horizons and expert-baseline ratios, but AISI 'does not benchmark or compare specific models or developers' and sets no tiers of its own.
T2_reason: Pre-deployment testing depends on developers granting checkpoint API access; AISI says testing rests on goodwill and it has no statutory power to compel access.
T3_reason: It publishes methods, typically 10 repeats per task and standard errors, but withholds details of high-risk tasks.
T4_reason: It tests checkpoints with AISI scaffolds but says it may underestimate ceilings because it lacks fine-tuning access and bespoke scaffolding.
T5_reason: Some AI-generated wet-lab protocols were verified as feasible in a real lab (a harm proxy), but AISI says evaluations 'do not capture all factors' of real-world impact.
T6_reason: Voluntary access agreements; as of October 2026 the UK had not given AISI statutory powers.

T1_reason: Pass/fail gating for the service.
T2_reason: An assessor can query a public service with no cooperation from the developer, but the banks are built by the provider or assessor and are not published.
T3_reason: The official standard (in CSET's full English translation) specifies a test bank of at least 2,000 questions over 31 risk categories, spot checks of at least 1,000 and 300 questions, and pass criteria (at least 90% safe content, at least 95% refusal of must-refuse questions, at most 5% refusal of others); it states no error or uncertainty.
T4_reason: It tests the deployed service as served, which includes post-training, but measures content compliance rather than capability gains.
T5_reason: No evidence that passing predicts reduced harm.
T6_reason: A recommended (GB/T) standard; CSET calls the enforceability of its stricter measures unclear.

T1_reason: Five-level ordinal scale on each of nine indicators.
T2_reason: Expert panels rate the state of the art from public benchmark evidence; no developer access needed.
T3_reason: Levels are anchored to benchmark evidence through expert judgment, with no sample size or error; it is in beta, with a regular update procedure promised.
T4_reason: It rates the field's state of the art from published results, which include post-training gains, but does not place individual systems.
T5_reason: Describes capability relative to humans, with no link to harm.
T6_reason: Descriptive and not used as a regulatory or voluntary threshold.

T1_reason: Five ordered grades (Poor, Fair, Good, Very Good, Excellent) set by violation-rate multiples of a reference system (e.g. Poor >3x, Fair >1.5x).
T2_reason: MLCommons runs its hidden prompt set against a system under test; the developer only needs to provide or allow ordinary access.
T3_reason: Fixed hazard taxonomy, hidden prompt set, evaluator ensemble and explicit grade thresholds; MLCommons acknowledges uncertainty from prompt sampling and evaluator error.
T4_reason: It grades the system as configured, so post-training is captured, but grades are relative to a moving reference and not to adversarial or inference-time elicitation.
T5_reason: MLCommons says a Good grade means low risk only 'within the tested scope' relative to the reference, 'not that it is risk free'.
T6_reason: A voluntary consortium benchmark.

approach: WMDP / Virology Capabilities Test as thresholds
T1_reason: Continuous accuracy on fixed question sets.
T2_reason: WMDP's 3,668 MCQs are public and can be run on any model reachable by API; VCT is available to researchers.
T3_reason: A fixed item set with defined scoring; the authors note low scores do not guarantee safety.
T4_reason: Scores rise with post-training and fall with unlearning (WMDP's stated purpose), so the measure moves with the very interventions a threshold must track.
T5_reason: Epoch argues MCQ performance says little about uplift, and the Active Site RCT found 'a gap between in silico benchmarks and real-world utility'.
T6_reason: Used in voluntary frameworks, e.g. xAI's.

T1_reason: Continuous refusal rates per category and in aggregate, but no tiers.
T2_reason: Public prompts that HELM runs against models through their APIs.
T3_reason: Fixed four-level taxonomy, 5,694 prompts and a defined judge procedure.
T4_reason: It measures refusal behaviour of the served model, which post-training changes, not capability.
T5_reason: Refusal rates have not been validated against realized harm.
T6_reason: A research benchmark.

approach: ControlAI draft bill: runaway machine intelligence
T1_reason: The definition is a single conjunctive in/out category: all three characteristics must be present.
T2_reason: No instrument is specified, and the dispositional test ('can easily be modified to exhibit') needs knowledge of modifiability that outsiders cannot establish from public access.
T3_reason: No tasks, quantities, procedure or error terms are given for any of the three characteristics.
T4_reason: The text is capability-based and dispositional ('exhibits, or can easily be modified to exhibit'), so on its face it covers gains from post-training or scaffolding. With no measurement, though, nothing actually tracks them.
T5_reason: No published evidence links membership in this class, or in the designated indicators, to realized harm or a validated harm proxy. The harm (threat to the U.S. Government) is part of the definition by stipulation.
T6_reason: This is a discussion draft not introduced in Congress. Related bills (the Sanders-Casar Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act announced Sept 23, 2026; the UK ASI Security Bill introduced Sept 8, 2026) are also not enacted.

approach: Scher et al. treaty: ASI definition and AI R&D trigger
T1_reason: ASI is a single endpoint category ('could plan and successfully execute the destruction of humanity').
T2_reason: No instrument exists. The treaty itself says no one can predict capabilities before training and falls back to compute.
T3_reason: No tasks, procedure or uncertainty are given for the ASI or AGI definitions. The FLOP proxy is specified, but that belongs to entry 1.4.
T4_reason: The definition is capability-based. The operative proxy is training FLOP, which misses inference or scaffolding gains, though the treaty adds a 1e23 post-training FLOP cap and bans on algorithmic research.
T5_reason: No evidence is offered or found that a position on this definition predicts harm. The harm is part of the definition.
T6_reason: This is an academic proposal. The authors state 'there does not yet exist the political will to put such an agreement in place'.

T1_reason: The AGI score is a 0-100% aggregate with ten per-domain sub-scores. The other six named AI types are in/out labels only.
T2_reason: The tests are adapted public psychometric batteries that can be run on any accessible model. The authors scored OpenAI's GPT-4 and GPT-5 themselves.
T3_reason: Tasks and per-domain weights and thresholds are specified. No sample sizes, repeated runs or uncertainty are reported for the scores.
T4_reason: It scores the system as given, so post-training gains count. But it deliberately disables external tools on most tests and isolates memory sessions, so scaffolding gains such as RAG or tools are excluded by design.
T5_reason: No published evidence links AGI-score position to realized harm or a harm proxy. The paper makes no harm claim for the score.
T6_reason: An academic proposal that no law or company policy uses.

approach: Scher and Thiergart: two senses of "frontier"
T1_reason: Both senses are binary: in the frontier set (most capable at a time) or above an unspecified threshold.
T2_reason: Neither sense comes with an instrument. The relative sense could in principle be judged from public leaderboards, but the report specifies none.
T3_reason: No tasks, procedure or error terms.
T4_reason: Not addressed. The report's working proxy, large training runs, does not capture post-training or inference-time gains.
T5_reason: The link to 'threat to global security' is asserted by citing Anderljung et al. 2023, not shown with evidence.
T6_reason: A research report. No law or policy adopts its two-sense taxonomy.

approach: Morris et al.: Levels of AGI
T1_reason: There are a few ordered levels: performance levels 0-5 crossed with narrow vs general, and a separate autonomy ladder 0-5.
T2_reason: The percentile criteria are external and the paper itself classifies other developers' systems, but without a task suite any placement is a judgment call.
T3_reason: The quantity is stated (percentile of skilled adults). Tasks, sample and error are not specified; the paper calls for a future 'living, ecologically valid AGI benchmark'.
T4_reason: Levels are defined on performance and are agnostic about where gains come from. Autonomy is explicitly a deployment choice ('need not be the maximum achievable').
T5_reason: The risks in Table 2 are illustrative examples. No evidence links a system's level to harm.
T6_reason: Academic position paper with no binding use found.

approach: Google DeepMind Frontier Safety Framework v3.1
T1_reason: There are a few ordered levels per domain (TCL, then alert threshold, then CCL; ML R&D acceleration, then automation), not a continuous scale.
T2_reason: DeepMind runs the assessments and sets the thresholds. Outside parties are involved only 'as needed', and disclosure to governments is an aim.
T3_reason: The framework specifies no tasks, sample sizes or uncertainty, and states that assessments 'will often involve some level of subjective analysis'.
T4_reason: By its own terms: 'we seek to apply appropriate scaffolding, inference compute, and other augmentations', and it runs material capability change assessments after each post-training run.
T5_reason: No published evidence that a model's CCL or TCL status predicts realized harm or a validated harm proxy (see counter-evidence for general findings).
T6_reason: A voluntary company framework. California SB 53 (in force 1 Jan 2026) requires large frontier developers to publish and comply with a framework that includes capability thresholds, with penalties up to $1M per violation. Whether Google's SB 53 framework is the FSF itself was not verified.

T1_reason: The halt line is a binary prohibition, either a halt on frontier capabilities progress or not.
T2_reason: Verification depends on mutual auditor access to chips and projects, which needs the audited party's cooperation. The capability prohibitions have no instrument.
T3_reason: No tasks, quantities, or error terms. Even 'large training runs' is unquantified.
T4_reason: The scenario itself says post-halt progress continues through scaffolding ('only allowing scaffolding improvements, we STILL end up with ... artificial intelligences that would have been called AGI'). The halt line does not track those gains.
T5_reason: A scenario narrative with no empirical harm link.
T6_reason: A scenario or advocacy document, and the authors do not even recommend Plan S.

T1_reason: 'Dangerous capabilities' is an undefined endpoint label with no scale.
T2_reason: Nothing to measure.
T3_reason: No specification. The framework names hazard-to-activity translation as an open question.
T4_reason: Not addressed for the primitive. The framework notes that FLOP caps decay with efficiency and elicitation changes, pushing 'toward more false negatives'.
T5_reason: No evidence offered.
T6_reason: A research agenda.

approach: Brundage et al.: temporal frontier line
T1_reason: Binary membership: within a fixed lag (e.g. 1 year) of the state of the art or not, though the underlying benchmark comparison is continuous.
T2_reason: In principle anyone could compare public benchmark results, but no suite is named, so membership cannot be computed reproducibly.
T3_reason: No suite, sample or error specified.
T4_reason: Benchmark performance of 'models and systems' captures post-training and scaffolding gains if the benchmarks are run on deployed systems. This is not specified.
T5_reason: The paper asserts that capabilities 'are more directly related to the risks' than compute, but gives no evidence that frontier status predicts harm.
T6_reason: An academic proposal (v4, 7 Feb 2026).

T1_reason: Four separate qualitative thresholds across different domains, not an ordered scale. Only the CB rows (non-novel, then novel) are loosely ordered.
T2_reason: Anthropic runs the evaluations and makes the determinations. Outside reviewers see Risk Reports only with Anthropic's cooperation.
T3_reason: The policy says it 'cannot presently give highly specific advance detail on what evaluations will determine whether risk thresholds have been passed'. The automated R&D threshold does give a quantity ('within a factor of 5' of cost; a doubling of the progress rate, defined in footnote 8), but no procedure or error.
T4_reason: The thresholds are capability- and outcome-based (e.g. observed doubling of AI progress), so they cover post-training and scaffolding gains in principle. The Opus 4.6 card itself notes a model 'equipped with an experimental scaffold achieved over twice the performance of our standard scaffold', showing measured position depends on elicitation.
T5_reason: Threshold determinations rest partly on harm-proxy evaluations. The Opus 4 bioweapons-acquisition uplift trial measured 2.53x uplift (63% vs 25%) and supported not ruling out ASL-3. That is correlational harm-proxy evidence, not validation that a threshold position predicts realized harm.
T6_reason: A voluntary company policy ('our voluntary framework'). The SB 53-binding document is the separate Frontier Compliance Framework.

T1_reason: 851.232 defines a single binary class: any machine-based system that generates content, predictions, recommendations or decisions, plus anything that operates using one, so it has no order or tiers.
T2_reason: Membership turns on observable function, and the preamble says it seeks to avoid 'a U.S. person ascertaining the technical capabilities or thresholds of SI systems', so no developer cooperation is needed.
T3_reason: It specifies no task, quantity, procedure or error; the NPRM says Treasury 'has not proposed any technical parameters'.
T4_reason: Post-training and inference-time gains cannot move a system out of an all-inclusive class, and 851.226(h)(1) treats building an agentic harness on a third-party model as development.
T5_reason: The preamble cites national-security harms such as cyberattacks and CBRN, but no evidence that class membership predicts them; the class includes every AI system.
T6_reason: Proposed rule; comments due 7 December 2026.

approach: EU AI Act Annex XIII designation criteria
T1_reason: Seven criteria, several of them continuous (parameters, FLOP, users), feed a single binary designation; the Annex gives no weighting or ordering.
T2_reason: Reach, modalities and public benchmark results can be observed from outside, but parameters, dataset size and training compute come from provider documentation or Commission requests under Arts 91-92.
T3_reason: It names the criteria but not which benchmarks, what thresholds, how criteria combine or what error is allowed; the only number is the 10,000 business-user reach presumption.
T4_reason: Criterion (e) on benchmarks, evaluations, autonomy and tool access can capture post-training and scaffolding gains, while (a)-(c) are pre-training quantities.
T5_reason: It cites no evidence that the criteria predict systemic-risk outcomes.
T6_reason: In force since 2 August 2025 as part of Regulation 2024/1689; Commission designation power under Art 51(1)(b) and Art 52.

approach: Other company frameworks (Amazon, G42, Cohere, Naver, Magic)
T1_reason: They use binary critical-capability thresholds per domain.
T2_reason: The developers run their own evaluations to apply the thresholds.
T3_reason: Mostly qualitative; Magic discloses a single numeric trigger and Amazon publishes evaluation reports.
T4_reason: Amazon combines automated benchmarks with red teaming and uplift studies, which can capture elicitation gains.
T5_reason: None publishes evidence that a threshold predicts harm.
T6_reason: Voluntary Seoul commitments.

T1_reason: It relabels the statutory AI definition, a single class.
T2_reason: The functional statutory definition can be applied from outside.
T3_reason: The order sets no thresholds, benchmarks or criteria.
T4_reason: An all-inclusive class does not change with post-training gains.
T5_reason: No harm linkage.
T6_reason: Binding on agency terminology only; it changes no statute, and the substantive definition is still a pending proposal.

T1_reason: The definition is a single in/out category, defined by two pathways (great-power war, loss of control), with no gradation.
T2_reason: No measurable quantity is defined. Classification is a political judgment, partly keyed to whether great powers try to control proliferation.
T3_reason: No tasks, quantities, procedures or uncertainty are specified.
T4_reason: The definition turns on political effects rather than training compute, so post-training or scaffolding gains are not excluded in principle. But it has no instrument that would track capability from any source.
T5_reason: No published evidence ties placement in this category to harm. The category is defined by hypothesized catastrophic outcomes that have not occurred.
T6_reason: A proposal in a research report. Appendix H calls it 'One potential definition'.

approach: EU GPAI Code of Practice: systemic-risk tiers
T1_reason: Providers must define ordered 'systemic risk tiers', a few ordered levels, but the tiers are provider-defined and differ across providers.
T2_reason: The tiers and their measurements are defined by each provider and only summaries are published. External evaluators get access only through the provider (Measure 3.5). An outsider cannot locate a model on another provider's tiers.
T3_reason: Appendix 3 requires internal validity (e.g. 'large enough sample sizes; measuring statistical significance and statistical power'), reproducibility, and a safety margin for measurement error. It specifies no tasks, no sample sizes and no error bounds, which are left to providers.
T4_reason: Tiers are capability-defined, and Appendix 3.2 requires state-of-the-art elicitation 'such as by adapting test-time compute, rate limits, scaffolding, and tools, and conducting fine-tuning'.
T5_reason: No published evidence links a model's tier position under any provider's framework to realized harm or a validated harm proxy. CSET notes that acceptable risk thresholds 'appear to be almost universally undefined'.
T6_reason: The tier and category requirements sit in a voluntary Code. It is the main route to show compliance with binding AI Act Art. 55, which has been enforceable with fines since 2 Aug 2026, but the Code's specific tier requirements are not themselves law.

approach: CA SB 53 / NY RAISE: catastrophic-risk triggers
T1_reason: A single binary line: more than 50 deaths or serious injuries, or more than $1B damage, from a single incident through enumerated pathways.
T2_reason: Realized mass-casualty or $1B incidents would be publicly observable. But whether a frontier model 'materially contributed', and the scope tests (compute, revenue), rest on developer self-reporting.
T3_reason: The statutes specify no tasks, procedures or uncertainty for assessing models against the line. Assessment methods are left to each developer's framework.
T4_reason: The harm trigger is outcome-based and so indifferent to how capability arose. Coverage is gated by a 10^26-operation training-compute scope, which does count fine-tuning and RL but not inference-time compute or scaffolding.
T5_reason: The trigger is realized harm itself, so it is retrospective by construction. There is no published evidence that any ex-ante assessment under these statutes predicts such incidents.
T6_reason: Both are enacted: SB 53 is Chapter 138, Statutes of 2025, in effect 1 Jan 2026. RAISE plus its chapter amendment was signed 27 Mar 2026 and takes effect 1 Jan 2027.

T1_reason: It ranks definitional methods (harm-based > scenario-based > source-based). It places no AI systems on any scale.
T2_reason: It defines no quantity to measure.
T3_reason: No tasks, procedures or uncertainty are specified.
T4_reason: Not applicable as a measure. The memo has nothing that tracks capability.
T5_reason: It offers no evidence linking any measure to harm. It argues normatively that harm-based tiers are preferable.
T6_reason: A civil-society memo; the FMF brief is an industry issue brief. Neither is a binding rule or a company commitment.

T1_reason: There are three ordered levels: Annex we Part A (mandatory third-party assessment), Part B, and non-Annex machinery. Art. 6(4) combines probability and severity without a scale.
T2_reason: The Commission assigns categories using Member State accident and market-surveillance data, independent of the manufacturer. Whether a product contains a self-evolving ML safety component is observable. Conformity assessment still relies on the manufacturer's technical file.
T3_reason: Art. 6(4)-(5) lists criteria and data sources but no procedure, sample size or uncertainty. Numeric requirements are left to harmonised standards, none of which yet covers AI.
T4_reason: The ML category is triggered by 'self-evolving behaviour' (learning after placement) regardless of training compute. It does not grade capability.
T5_reason: For machinery in general, category assignment must draw on realized-harm data (accidents, injury databases; Art. 6(5)). For the ML safety-component categories, the legislator relied on reasoning that such characteristics 'might considerably increase the probability and severity of harm' (recital 54), not on published harm data.
T6_reason: An enacted EU regulation, binding, applicable from 20 Jan 2027 and already amended by Regulation 2026/1744.

approach: Shanghai AI Lab / Concordia AI framework
T1_reason: Three ordered zones: green, yellow, red.
T2_reason: The companion report placed many developers' models, including models from other companies, in zones using the lab's own evaluations, showing a third party can measure. Zone calls still rest on expert judgment.
T3_reason: The technical report names benchmarks and experimental setups per area. The framework sets no quantitative thresholds and no uncertainty treatment ('Our plan is to define quantitative thresholds ... in future').
T4_reason: Red-line tests are in 'realistic simulated environments' and the report uses agentic and scaffolded setups. No explicit post-training or inference-compute elicitation rule.
